R001.text: Fix a metric space X, a subset A⊆X and s>0. Regard its metric as an extended metric and give X its Borel measurable structure. M001 gives the native covering formula. At every finite positive scale its inner infimum is exactly Hscale(s,δ,A): extended diameter agrees with ordinary diameter on bounded sets, nonempty-member costs agree, and both conventions make empty members zero. Infinite-diameter sets cannot occur at a finite scale. The extra scale r=∞ in M001 contributes no more than any finite-scale infimum because its cover class is larger. Thus its inclusion does not change the supremum over finite positive scales. Hence Hnative(s,A)=Hmeasure(s,A).

Using F001, apply M002 in the case s<hdim(A) to obtain Hmeasure(s,A)=∞. Apply M003 in the case hdim(A)<s to obtain Hmeasure(s,A)=0. If Hmeasure(s,A)=0, F001 makes Hnative(s,A)=0≠∞, so M004 gives hdim(A)≤s. If Hmeasure(s,A)=∞, then F001 and the supremum definition of hdim show s≤hdim(A), since s is one of its nonnegative exponents with infinite native measure. Each implication is conditional only on its displayed antecedent and is closed here; X,A,s were arbitrary. This proves every asserted clause.

R002.text: By H002 and the finite-open-subcover definition of compactness, the increasing open balls about 0 of positive integer radii have a finite subcover of E. These balls cover Euclidean space because every point has finite norm. Adjoin the radius-one ball if necessary so that the finite family is nonempty. The maximum of its radii bounds all norms in E, proving boundedness. Define B=max(1,sup{‖x‖₂:x∈E}), using the total real supremum convention (zero on empty or unbounded-above sets). The boundedness just proved and the least-upper-bound property give ‖x‖₂≤B for all x∈E, and B≥1. Also, for any δ>0, the open balls of radius δ/2 about points of E form an open cover; compactness supplies a finite subcover. Each ball has diameter at most δ by the triangle inequality and hence finite s-cost for every s>0. A finite sum of these costs is finite, so the defining infimum gives Hscale(s,δ,E)<∞.

Always D≥0 by its extended-nonnegative-real definition. If n>0, E lies in the box [-B,B]^n by F001. For each 0<h≤1, use the ordinary grid of mesh h and retain cubes intersecting this box. There are at most (2B/h+3)^n≤(2B+3)^n h^{-n} such cubes, each of side h and Euclidean diameter at most √n h (sum the n coordinate squared differences). Writing C=(2B+3)^n, for every real exponent a>n their total a-cost is at most C n^{a/2}h^{a-n}→0 as h↓0. At any fixed target scale, all sufficiently small h are admissible and these costs tend to zero; thus Hscale(a,δ,E)=0 for every δ>0 and Hmeasure(a,E)=0. N001 gives D≤a for every a>n, hence D≤n. If n=0, H001 makes E the whole singleton ℝ^0. Its singleton cover has zero s-cost for every s>0 at every positive scale. N001 gives D≤s for all s>0, hence D=0. This proves the claimed bound and the exceptional-case identification; since n is finite, D is finite. Together with the preceding paragraph this proves every asserted clause.

R003.text: First suppose n=0. N002 gives E=ℝ^0 and D=0. With the Euclidean metric in D002, F is isometric to I. For each positive integer N, divide I into N closed pieces of length 1/N and use their copies in F. For any a>1, their total a-cost is N(1/N)^a=N^{1-a}→0 as N→∞, while their diameters tend to zero. Thus at each target scale δ_0>0, Hscale(a,δ_0,F)=0 and Hmeasure(a,F)=0. N001 gives hdim(F)≤a for all a>1, so hdim(F)≤1=D+1. This closes the n=0 branch.

Now suppose n≥1. N002 permits regarding D as a finite real number. Fix q>D, a target scale δ>0 and ε>0, and set r=min(1,δ/√2). Since D≥0, q>0. N001 gives Hmeasure(q,E)=0, hence Hscale(q,r,E)=0. The definition of infimum supplies a countable r-cover of cost less than ε/2. Delete empty members. Every remaining diameter-zero member is a singleton. Replace its member with original index i≥0 by a ball centered at that singleton, of positive diameter at most r and q-cost less than ε2^{-i-2}. Such a ball exists in ℝ^n for n≥1: take a sufficiently small positive radius, using (2a)^q→0 as a↓0. The sum of all added costs is at most Σ_{i≥0}ε2^{-i-2}=ε/2, and in fact the resulting total cost is less than ε. Keep the positive-diameter original members. This proves the existence of a countable cover of E with every member nonempty, 0<diam U_i≤r and Σ_i(diam U_i)^q<ε.

Choose U by F001, and put r_i=diam U_i and N_i=ceil(1/r_i). Partition I into the N_i closed intervals [(j-1)/N_i,j/N_i], 1≤j≤N_i. They have length 1/N_i≤r_i. As 0<r_i≤r≤1, one has N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The sets T_{i,j}=U_i×[(j-1)/N_i,j/N_i] form a countable cover of F. The Euclidean product distance gives diam T_{i,j}≤√2 r_i≤δ. Their total (q+1)-cost is bounded by Σ_i N_i(√2 r_i)^{q+1}≤2(√2)^{q+1}Σ_i r_i^q<2(√2)^{q+1}ε. Consequently Hscale(q+1,δ,F)≤2(√2)^{q+1}ε.

The bound F002 holds for every ε>0, at the arbitrary positive scale δ and arbitrary q>D. Taking ε↓0 gives Hscale(q+1,δ,F)=0. Taking the supremum over all δ>0 gives Hmeasure(q+1,F)=0, and N001 yields hdim(F)≤q+1 for every q>D. Since D is finite by N002, letting q↓D gives hdim(F)≤D+1 (equivalently, any larger number would admit an intermediate q+1 contradicting these bounds). Close the restrictions q>D, δ>0, ε>0 and the n≥1 case. Together with the zero-dimensional branch this proves the upper bound.

R004.text: Fix s>0, δ>0 and ε>0. Define c=Hscale(s,δ,E). N002 gives a finite δ-cover of E with finite s-cost, so c<∞. Thus c can be integrated as a finite nonnegative constant.

Take any countable δ-cover V of F and write ρ_i=diam V_i, A_i=π_{ℝ^n}(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Coordinate projections decrease distances by the Euclidean distance formula; therefore diam A_i≤ρ_i and diam B_i≤ρ_i≤δ. Set η_i=ε2^{-i-1}/(1+ρ_i^s)>0. For every nonempty V_i its projection B_i is nonempty and bounded: distances between all its points are at most δ, so its infimum and supremum are finite. Their difference is at most ρ_i. Define J_i=(inf B_i-η_i/2,sup B_i+η_i/2), which contains B_i and has length at most ρ_i+η_i. For empty V_i set J_i=∅; such members have ρ_i^s=0 and are harmless. This is the same as discarding empty members while retaining the original indices. Thus every J_i is open and B_i⊆J_i. Neither V_i nor its projections need be measurable.

For any t∈I, the A_i with t∈J_i cover E: for any x∈E some V_i contains (x,t), and then x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. By F002 this is a δ-cover, whose s-cost is at most Σ_iρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). Hence c≤Σ_iρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t) for every t∈I. Define f_i(t)=ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). Every f_i is nonnegative and Borel measurable because J_i is open and its coefficient is a fixed finite nonnegative real. In particular it is almost-everywhere measurable for Lebesgue measure restricted to I.

Integrate F003 against Lebesgue measure restricted to I. Its total mass is one by M007 with endpoints 0,1. Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral, the integral of a constant, and M005 applied to the nonnegative measurable series yield c≤Σ_i∫_I f_i(t)dt=Σ_iρ_i^s|J_i∩I|. Here the integral of a constant times a measurable indicator is that constant times its set's measure, directly the simple-function integral formula. By M008 and monotonicity of measure, |J_i∩I|≤|J_i|≤ρ_i+η_i (the empty case is zero). Consequently c≤Σ_iρ_i^s|J_i∩I|≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1}+Σ_iη_iρ_i^s≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1}+ε, because η_iρ_i^s=ε2^{-i-1}ρ_i^s/(1+ρ_i^s)≤ε2^{-i-1} and Σ_{i≥0}2^{-i-1}=1. All series are nonnegative; their order comparisons and splitting are valid also when a sum is infinite.

If Σ_iρ_i^{s+1}=∞, the desired bound c≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1} is immediate. If the sum is finite, F004 for all ε>0 gives that bound by letting ε↓0. Since V was any δ-cover of F, taking the infimum of its (s+1)-costs gives Hscale(s,δ,E)=c≤Hscale(s+1,δ,F). The construction of J depended on ε, but c and this cover's cost did not, so the limit is legitimate. Discharge the arbitrary-cover restrictions and s>0,δ>0,ε>0 restrictions and universally quantify s,δ. This proves the slicing inequality.

R005.text: Suppose D>0 and fix 0<s<D. By N001, Hmeasure(s,E)=∞. Thus Hscale(s,δ,E) is arbitrarily large as δ↓0: it increases when the allowed scale decreases, since the class of covers becomes smaller, and its supremum over positive scales is infinite. For every δ>0, N004 gives Hscale(s,δ,E)≤Hscale(s+1,δ,F). Therefore the supremum over scales on the right is infinite, so Hmeasure(s+1,F)=∞. N001 then gives hdim(F)≥s+1.

N002 makes D finite. Under D>0, the positive exponents s<D approach D from below. F001 therefore yields hdim(F)≥D+1 by order completeness; explicitly any number less than D+1 is less than s+1 for some 0<s<D. Close the assumption D>0 to obtain the asserted implication.

R006.text: First establish the dimension of I. For every positive integer N its subdivision into N equal closed intervals is a cover with diameters 1/N. For every a>1, its total a-cost is N^{1-a}→0 as N→∞. These covers have mesh tending to zero, so Hmeasure(a,I)=0. By N001, hdim(I)≤a for all a>1 and therefore hdim(I)≤1.

Fix δ>0 and any countable δ-cover W of I, and set ρ_i=diam W_i≤δ. For arbitrary ε>0, enclose each nonempty W_i in J_i=(inf W_i-ε2^{-i-2},sup W_i+ε2^{-i-2}); its endpoints are finite because W_i is nonempty and bounded. Its length is at most ρ_i+ε2^{-i-1}; set J_i=∅ for empty W_i. The J_i cover I. By M007, the length of I is 1; monotonicity and M006 give 1≤Σ_i|J_i|. M008 bounds this by Σ_iρ_i+Σ_iε2^{-i-1}=Σ_iρ_i+ε. If Σ_iρ_i is infinite the claimed bound is immediate; otherwise let ε↓0 to get Σ_iρ_i≥1. Close the arbitrary choices to conclude that for every δ>0, every countable δ-cover of I has sum of diameters at least one.

Fix any 0<s<1, δ_1>0 and any δ_1-cover W_1 of I, with diameters (ρ_1)_i≤δ_1. One has (ρ_1)_i^s≥δ_1^{s-1}(ρ_1)_i; at (ρ_1)_i=0 both sides are zero, and for (ρ_1)_i>0 this follows since the exponent s-1 is negative. Thus F002 gives Σ_i(ρ_1)_i^s≥δ_1^{s-1}Σ_i(ρ_1)_i≥δ_1^{s-1}. Taking the infimum over the arbitrary covers W_1 yields Hscale(s,δ_1,I)≥δ_1^{s-1}→∞ as δ_1↓0. Hence Hmeasure(s,I)=∞ and N001 gives hdim(I)≥s for every 0<s<1. Let s↑1 to obtain hdim(I)≥1, which together with F001 proves hdim(I)=1. All cover and exponent quantifiers have been closed.

Suppose D=0. Choose x_0∈E by H001 and define φ:I→F by φ(t)=(x_0,t). The Euclidean distance formula gives dist(φ(t),φ(u))=|t-u|, so this is an isometric embedding, also when n=0. To justify the dimension monotonicity being used, fix b>0, δ_2>0 and any countable δ_2-cover Q of F. Define Qpre_i={t∈I:φ(t)∈Q_i}. These preimages cover I, and diam Qpre_i≤diam Q_i because distances of preimage points equal distances of their images. Empty preimages contribute zero. Hence Hscale(b,δ_2,I) is at most the b-cost of Q. Taking the infimum over all Q proves Hscale(b,δ_2,I)≤Hscale(b,δ_2,F) for every b>0,δ_2>0, and taking suprema gives Hmeasure(b,I)≤Hmeasure(b,F) for all b>0. Close these cover, scale and exponent quantifiers. By F003 and N001, Hmeasure(a,I)=∞ for every 0<a<1, hence Hmeasure(a,F)=∞ and hdim(F)≥a. Let a↑1 to get hdim(F)≥1=hdim(I). Since D=0 this is 1=D+1. Here D=0 itself supplies its finite-real interpretation, and no step required n>0. Discharge D=0 to prove the asserted implication.

R007.text: By N002, 0≤D≤n, so D is finite and either D>0 or D=0. In the first case N005 gives hdim(F)≥D+1; in the second N006 gives exactly the same lower bound. Thus hdim(F)≥D+1 in all cases. N003 gives the reverse bound. By antisymmetry hdim(F)=D+1=hdim(E)+1, as required. The definition of F supplies precisely E×[0,1] in the Euclidean metric, including n=0.
